dataset.name: Arctic shrub root traits, northern Alaska, summer 2017 (Version 2.0)
description: This data package contains root trait data collected from 170 plots of rapidly expanding shrub genera (Alnus, Betula, and Salix) and a widespread sedge (Eriophorum vaginatum) along a latitudinal and temperature gradient in northern Alaska. The trait data were collected in July 2017 and include root architecture (root diameter and branching patterns), mycorrhizal colonization (%), nitrogen concentration (%), delta 15N (per mil), and vertical root biomass. These raw data support a submitted manuscript that examines the distribution and interspecific variations of absorptive root traits of shrubs and graminoids across the graminoid-dominated nutrient-poor arctic tundra and reveals how deciduous shrub expansion affects plant nutrient acquisition strategies in tundra ecosystems. Data are presented by site (n=5) and patch (shrub or sedge plot) in separate csv files. The location data are provided in the “plot coordinates” file; all other files contain the data in the file title. Detailed methods are in Chen et al. (2020).

2023/07/20 Update: The latest version of this dataset publication is version 2.0. The latest version of the data package was updated to include the alder nodule biomass dataset (alder nodule biomass.csv) and associated metadata (metadata_alder nodule biomass.csv). The name of the previous metadata file was updated (metadata_ root traits and biomass.csv ) to distinguish it from the new metadata file.

measurementTechnique:
1. Root samples for trait measurements were sampled in the upper 20 cm of soil.
2. Only absorptive roots were included in trait measurements. The first three root orders were determined as absorptive roots for shrubs. Because Eriophorum roots do not have branching architecture, all individual Eriophorum root segments containing root tips were considered as absorptive roots.
3. Root vertical distribution in the active layer was estimated using a 7.6-cm-diameter soil corer. Depth of the moss layer before it was removed from the soil core. Only live roots included.
4. To determine alder nodule biomass, four soil cores were collected around the base of each alder shrub within the plot. Cores were collected to a depth of 10 cm using a 3.5-cm diameter corer.
4. Detailed methods are provided below and in: Chen, W. L., K. D. Tape, E. S. Euskirchen, S. Liang, A. Matos, J. Greenberg, and J. M. Fraterrigo. 2020. Impacts of arctic shrubs on root traits and belowground nutrient cycles across a northern Alaskan climate gradient. Frontiers in Plant Science 11:588098.

Study sites
In June and July of 2017, we selected five sampling sites along a latitudinal gradient in Northern Alaska (67.0 °N – 69.3 °N), encompassing a wide range of summer soil temperature (5.2 °C – 8.9 °C). Based on satellite image data (supplementary methods), all of the five sites showed a long-term increase of vegetation greenness, consistent with the observed expansion of shrub abundance in many Alaskan tundra areas (Jia, Epstein, & Walker, 2003; Ju & Masek, 2016). At each sampling site, we identified species from three expanding deciduous shrub genera Alnus (A. viridis ssp. fruticosa), Betula (B. nana), and Salix (S. glauca, S. pulchra, S. arbuscoloides, or S. richardsonii), respectively alder, birch, and willow. For each selected shrub genera, we established nine plots in each site. We also selected seven tussock sedge plots in each site that were dominated by Eriophorum vaginatum and close to the shrub plots, resulting in 170 sampled plots across the Northern Alaskan sampling transect. All plots were 1-m-diameter circles surrounding the stem of the selected shrub individual or the tussock sedge. Percentages of vegetation cover of the three shrubs and graminoids were estimated for each plot. In shrub plots, the target shrub was that which showed the largest cover among the three shrub genera; while in sedge plots, shrub cover was almost negligible.
Root trait measurements
We harvested root samples from the target plant for trait measurements in the upper 20 cm of soil in each plot. In shrub plots, we excavated intact root branches linked to the target shrub individual. At least six intact root branches, including the 1st to 6th (or higher) orders (sensu Guo et al. 2008) were carefully cut and stored in coolers before returning to the lab. In sedge plots, the live roots (light color and dense tissue) that connected to the tussock of E. vaginatum were also cut and stored. All root and leaf samples were kept at -20 °C in the lab until processing.
Roots were carefully rinsed with deionized water to remove soil particles. We considered the first three root orders as absorptive roots for shrubs (sensu McCormack et al., 2015). Because E. vaginatum roots do not have branching architecture, all individual E. vaginatum root segments containing root tips were considered absorptive roots. A subset of approximately fifteen absorptive roots from each plot was selected for scanning on a desktop scanner. All scanned root images were processed with WinRHIZO (Regent Instruments, Quebec, Canada) to determine the average root diameter. Root architectures were also determined from scanned images. The number of 1st, 2nd, and 3rd order roots was counted in each image, and branching ratios were calculated as the number of 1st-order roots per each 2nd-order root (BR1-2) and the number of 2nd-order roots per each 3rd-order root (BR2-3). The scanned roots were oven-dried at 55 °C for 72 hours and ground to a fine powder. Root tissue nitrogen concentration ([N]), as well as N isotopic signature δ15N, was determined using a Costech 4010 CHNSO Elemental Analyzer (Costech Analytical Technologies Inc., Valencia, CA, USA) interfaced with an isotope ratio mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Delta V Advantage, Fisher Scientific) at the University of Illinois. Another subset of fresh root sample was preserved in 70% (v/v) ethanol for later determination of the percentage of root tips that were colonized by ectomycorrhizal fungi by inspection of root tip morphology, color, architecture, and anatomy.
Root biomass and vertical distribution
Within each plot, an intact soil core (moss + organic + mineral layer) was manually sampled using a 7.6-cm-diameter soil corer with a post driver until reaching the permafrost layer. The intact soil core was wrapped using aluminum foil in the field. Soil cores were stored in coolers until transferred to -20 °C freezers. The depth of the resulting hole was measured. In the lab, soil cores were carefully placed on the bench. The moss layer (if any) usually rapidly reshaped and we measured the depth of the moss layer before it was removed from the soil core. The remaining soil core was separated into the organic and mineral layers based on the visible differences in organic matter content. Some cores contained only an organic or mineral layer. Lengths of the organic and mineral layers were measured. The soil core was then sliced into two halves, with one half reserved for later soil analysis. The other half was used to quantify absorptive root biomass. This half soil core was cut into 2-cm thick pieces, labeled by position within the soil core (i.e. core depth) and converted to field depth to adjust for compression during sampling:
Dfield = Dcore × (Lhole-Lmoss)/(Lcore-Lmoss),
Where Dfield is the depth of a soil-piece in the field (excluding moss layer), and Dcore is its depth measured in the lab. Lhole is the total length of the hole resulting from soil coring to the permafrost, and Lcore is the length of the intact cores (moss layer + organic layer + mineral layer) measured in the lab. Lmoss is the length of the moss layer (if any).
After soil cores were divided into different depth increments, all roots from each depth increment were carefully picked and rinsed. Because roots of different plant species inside and outside the plot could intermix at fine scales, and because of the difficulty in differentiating roots among species, the root biomass at different depths represents root vertical distribution at a plant-community level. In particular, only live roots (based on root color, surface structure, and tissue density) were collected. Roots were further separated into absorptive vs. non-absorptive (woody) roots based on woody structures and root orders. Both absorptive and non-absorptive roots were oven-dried at 55 °C for 72 hours and weighed. The depth increment of each sample and the inner core radius was used to calculate root biomass density at different soil depths. In total, we collected and measured the absorptive root biomass from 1172 pieces of soil core sections.
Alder nodule biomass
To determine alder nodule biomass, four soil cores were collected around the base of each alder shrub within the plot. Cores were collected to a depth of 10 cm using a 3.5-cm diameter corer. Cores were composited, placed on ice for transport, and frozen. For each 1-m diameter plot, we measured the height of the tallest alder stem to the nearest cm, and the basal diameter of all alder stems using digital calipers. In the laboratory, each composite sample was thoroughly searched and any live nodules were collected. Nodules were rinsed with DI water and placed in labeled envelopes for drying @70C for 48 h.
